title: Reading a regression summary
objectives: Explain every number in a statsmodels summary table.
Fit a line with statsmodels and read its coefficients, errors and $R^2$

screens.title: A real summary
screens.prose: We regressed 60 hourly stock returns, in basis points, on an order-flow signal. The call was `sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()`, and this is its `summary()`.

lines: [1] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.

screens.question: Tap the line that holds the signal's slope.

hints.text: The slope is a coefficient. Look in the middle block.
The middle block has one row per coefficient.
One row is named after the predictor, `signal`.

feedback.correct: The `signal` row holds the slope: 3.85 bp per unit of signal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the row named after the predictor.

byKey.l15: That row is `const`, the intercept: the fitted return when the signal is 0.
byKey.l3: That line holds $R^2$, how much of the variance the line explains. The slope is in the coefficient block.
byKey.l13: That is the header of the coefficient block. The slope is in the row below it named `signal`.

explain.text: The `signal` row holds its coefficient, 3.849, then its standard error, $t$, $p$-value and 95% interval. The `const` row holds the same five numbers for the intercept. Everything else describes the fit as a whole.

screens.title: Reading a row
screens.prose: The columns are `coef`, `std err`, `t`, `P>|t|` and the 95% interval. Check that they hang together.

screens.question: Divide the signal's `coef` by its `std err`. What do you get?

hints.text: Read the two numbers from the `signal` row.
coef is 3.8492 and std err is 1.301.

byKey.flip: You divided std err by coef. The $t$ statistic puts the coefficient on top.
byKey.const: You read the `const` row. Use the `signal` row.

explain.text: $t = 3.849 / 1.301 = 2.959$, and `P>|t|` is its two-sided $p$-value on 58 degrees of freedom. The interval is $3.849 \pm 2.002 \times 1.301$, from 1.246 to 6.453. Each row is the last two lessons in one line.

screens.title: Every other number
screens.prose: Step through the rest of the table. Each step shades the lines it explains.

lines: [1] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.

steps.caption: **R-squared** is the share of the variance of `ret_bp` the line explains: 13.1%. **Adj. R-squared** corrects it for the number of predictors.
**F-statistic** tests every slope at once. With one predictor it is $t^2 = 2.959^2 = 8.76$, and **Prob (F-statistic)** equals the slope's $p$-value.
**No. Observations** is $n = 60$. **Df Model** counts predictors, $k = 1$. **Df Residuals** is $n - k - 1 = 58$, the degrees of freedom of every $t$.
**Log-Likelihood**, **AIC** and **BIC** score the fit for comparing models. Lower AIC or BIC is better. **Covariance Type** nonrobust means the usual standard errors.
**Omnibus** and **Jarque-Bera** test whether the residuals look normal: $p$ of 0.64 and 0.62, no alarm. **Skew** and **Kurtosis** describe their shape: normal is 0 and 3.
**Durbin-Watson** near 2 means no autocorrelation in the residuals (level 3). **Cond. No.** warns of collinearity. The residual standard error is not printed: it is `np.sqrt(res.scale)`, 7.85 bp.

screens.title: Adjusted R-squared
screens.prose: Adding any predictor, even pure noise, never lowers $R^2$. The adjusted version charges for each one: $$\bar R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n - 1}{n - k - 1},$$ with $k$ predictors. Here $R^2 = 0.1312$.

params.title: res.summary(): ret_bp on signal
lines: [1] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.

screens.question: Compute $\bar R^2$ for this fit, with $n = 60$ and $k = 1$.

hints.text: Start with $1 - R^2 = 0.8688$.

feedback.correct: 0.116, as printed on the Adj. R-squared line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $1 - R^2$ by $59/58$ and subtract from 1.

byKey.raw: That is $R^2$ itself. The adjustment scales $1 - R^2$ up by $59/58$.
byKey.by-n: You used $n/(n - k - 1) = 60/58$. The top of the factor is $n - 1 = 59$.
byKey.k: You charged for two predictors. Df Model is $k = 1$; the intercept is already in the $-1$.

explain.text: $1 - 0.8688 \times 59/58 = 0.116$. Each extra predictor shrinks $n - k - 1$, so it must cut SSE enough to pay its way. A new predictor raises $\bar R^2$ only when its $|t|$ exceeds 1.

screens.title: Which degrees of freedom?
screens.prose: Every $t$ statistic and $p$-value in the table uses the degrees of freedom of $s$.

screens.question: Tap the line that gives the degrees of freedom of the $t$ tests.

hints.text: Two lines start with Df.
One counts predictors, the other what is left for the residuals.
The $t$ tests use $n - 2$, which is 58 here.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line showing $n - 2$.

byKey.l10: Df Model is 1, the number of predictors. The $t$ tests use what is left: Df Residuals.
byKey.l8: That is $n = 60$. Two degrees of freedom went on the intercept and slope.

explain.text: Df Residuals $= n - k - 1 = 58$ is the divisor in $s^2 = \mathrm{SSE}/58$. It is also the degrees of freedom of every $t$ in the coefficient block. Df Model, 1, is the numerator's degrees of freedom for $F$.

screens.title: Is the model useless?
screens.prose: A colleague reads `P>|t|` = 0.558 on the first coefficient row. They conclude the model explains nothing.

screens.question: Tap one line that actually tests whether the model explains anything.

hints.text: Which coefficient does the 0.558 belong to?
The first row is the intercept. The test of the whole model is in the top block.
Prob (F-statistic) tests all slopes together.

feedback.correct: The $F$ test, or the slope's $t$, answers it: $p = 0.004$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the test of the slopes, not of the intercept.

byKey.l15: That is the intercept's test: is the average return zero when the signal is 0? It says nothing about the signal.
byKey.l3: $R^2$ measures how much is explained, but it is not a test. The $F$ line tests it.

explain.text: 0.558 is the $p$-value of `const`: it asks whether the return is zero when the signal is 0. The model's test is $F = 8.76$ with $p = 0.0045$. With one predictor that is the slope's own test.

screens.title: No constant
screens.prose: Someone fitted the same data with `sm.OLS(y, x)`, forgetting `add_constant`. The line is forced through the origin.

params.title: res.summary() without add_constant
lines: [1] R² is computed without centering (uncentered) since the model does not contain a constant.
[2] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.

screens.question: Tap one line that shows the model has no intercept.

hints.text: Compare with the first table. What is missing or renamed?
Look at the $R^2$ lines and the coefficient block.
The $R^2$ line now says uncentered.

feedback.correct: The uncentered $R^2$, the lone `signal` row and Df Residuals of 59 all give it away.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for what differs from the table with a constant.

explain.text: Without a constant the slope moves from 3.85 to 3.91 and Df Residuals rises to 59. $R^2$ is now uncentred: it compares the fit with $\sum y_i^2$, not $\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2$. It cannot be compared with 0.131, and with a large mean in $y$ it can sit near 1 for a poor fit.

screens.title: Why $F = t^2$
screens.prose: With one predictor, the explained sum of squares is $\mathrm{ESS} = \sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2$, and $F = \mathrm{ESS}/s^2$. Show it equals $t^2$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\mathrm{ESS} = \hat\beta^2 \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = \hat\beta^2 S_{xx}$: each $\hat y_i - \bar y = \hat\beta (x_i - \bar x)$
$F = \left(\dfrac{\hat\beta}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)}\right)^2 = t^2$: the denominator is the slope's standard error

hints.text: Start from the definition of $F$.
The fitted line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, which gives $\hat y_i - \bar y$.
Definition, ESS in terms of $\hat\beta$, regroup, recognise SE.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the definition and substitute ESS before regrouping.

byKey.f3: Regrouping needs ESS written as $\hat\beta^2 S_{xx}$ first.
byKey.f4: Recognising the standard error is the last step.

explain.text: The fitted values sit on a line through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, so ESS is $\hat\beta^2 S_{xx}$. Dividing by $s^2$ gives the square of $\hat\beta/\mathrm{SE}$. With several predictors $F$ tests them jointly and no single $t$ matches it.

screens.title: Fit it yourself
screens.prose: Now run the fit. `res.params` and `res.bse` hold the coefficients and their standard errors, constant first. `res.rsquared` is $R^2$.
screens.question: Complete `fit_line` so it returns $[\hat\alpha, \hat\beta, \mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha), \mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta), R^2]$, each rounded to 4 places.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

def fit_line(x, y):
    X = ...      # a column of ones, then x
    res = ...    # fit y on X by OLS
    vals = [*res.params, *res.bse, res.rsquared]
    return [round(float(v), 4) for v in vals]
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

def fit_line(x, y):
    X = sm.add_constant(np.array(x, dtype=float))
    res = sm.OLS(np.array(y, dtype=float), X).fit()
    vals = [*res.params, *res.bse, res.rsquared]
    return [round(float(v), 4) for v in vals]
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, including the 60 hours from this lesson, and compares each of the 5 numbers with math.isclose. statsmodels is large: the first run loads it with NumPy, SciPy and pandas, which takes 20 to 40 seconds.

hints.text: `sm.add_constant(x)` puts a column of ones before `x`.
`sm.OLS(y, X).fit()` returns the results object.
`X = sm.add_constant(np.array(x, dtype=float))`, then `res = sm.OLS(np.array(y, dtype=float), X).fit()`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check that `X` has the column of ones and that `y` comes first in `sm.OLS`.

explain.text: `add_constant` is what puts $\hat\alpha$ in the model. `sm.OLS` takes `y` first, then `X`. The rounded values match the printed table: 0.5985, 3.8492, 1.017, 1.301 and 0.131.

screens.title: A factor regression
screens.prose: A fund's monthly excess return, in %, regressed on three factors: the market (`mkt`), small minus big (`smb`) and value minus growth (`hml`). Five years of data.

params.title: res.summary(): fund_xs on three factors
lines: [1] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.

screens.question: Which sentence reads the `hml` coefficient correctly?

options.text: When value beats growth by 1% in a month, the fund tends to return 0.28% less, other factors fixed
The fund loses 0.28% a month from its value exposure
options.why: You read a sensitivity as a return. The fund loses only in months when value beats growth.

options.text: The fund and the value factor are negatively correlated, so $\beta_{hml} = -0.28$ is its correlation
options.why: A coefficient is a slope in % per %, not a correlation. It also holds the other factors fixed.

options.text: The coefficient is not significant, so the fund has no value tilt
options.why: You read the wrong column. $t = -4.66$ and $p = 0.000$: the tilt is clear.

hints.text: A coefficient is a slope: the change in $y$ per unit change in its factor.
Read the `hml` row: coef $-0.2765$, $t = -4.66$.
Negative means the fund does worse when value beats growth, holding mkt and smb fixed.

feedback.correct: A growth tilt: $-0.28$% per 1% of value premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the coefficient as % of fund return per 1% of factor return.

explain.text: Each coefficient is a sensitivity with the other factors held fixed. The fund gains 0.98% per 1% of market and 0.39% per 1% of `smb`: a small-cap tilt. Its alpha, `const`, is $-0.007$% a month with $p = 0.965$: no evidence of skill.

ideas: Each coefficient row is coef, std err, $t = $ coef/std err, its two-sided $p$-value on Df Residuals, and the 95% interval.
$R^2$ is the share of variance explained; adjusted $R^2$ charges for each predictor. The $F$ test checks all slopes at once, and equals $t^2$ with one predictor.
Without `add_constant` the line goes through the origin and the $R^2$ printed is uncentred.

formula.name: Adjusted R-squared
formula.note: A new predictor raises $\bar R^2$ only if its $|t| > 1$.

summary.trap: The `const` row's $p$-value tests the intercept, not the model. Read Prob (F-statistic) for that.

quiz.prose: A summary shows `const` with `P>|t|` = 0.40 and the only predictor with `P>|t|` = 0.001.
quiz.question: Which reading is right?

options.text: The predictor is strongly related to $y$; the intercept may be zero
The model is weak, because its first $p$-value is 0.40
options.why: You read the intercept's $p$-value as the model's. The model's test is the slope's or the $F$ test.

options.text: The two $p$-values average to 0.2, so nothing is significant
options.why: $p$-values are not averaged. Each row tests its own coefficient.

options.text: Drop the predictor: its $p$-value is the smaller one
options.why: You flipped the rule. A small $p$-value is evidence the coefficient is not zero.

feedback.correct: Each row tests its own coefficient.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which coefficient each $p$-value belongs to.

explain.text: 0.40 tests the intercept: is the mean of $y$ zero when $x$ is 0? 0.001 tests the slope, and with one predictor it equals Prob (F-statistic).

quiz.prose: A regression with $k = 3$ predictors on $n = 25$ points has $R^2 = 0.30$.
quiz.question: What is the adjusted $R^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - k - 1)$.

byKey.raw: That is $R^2$. The adjustment charges for three predictors.
byKey.by-n: You used $n = 25$ on top. The factor is $(n - 1)/(n - k - 1) = 24/21$.

explain.text: $(n - 1)/(n - k - 1) = 24/21 = 1.143$, so $\bar R^2 = 1 - 0.70 \times 1.143 = 0.20$. Three predictors cost a third of the apparent fit.

quiz.prose: A regression with one predictor reports the slope's $t = -2.5$.
quiz.question: What F-statistic does the summary show?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one predictor $F = t^2$.

explain.text: With one predictor $F = t^2 = 6.25$, and its $p$-value equals the slope's two-sided $p$-value. The sign of the slope is lost in the square.

quiz.prose: Two return models are fitted on the same ten years. Model A has adjusted $R^2 = 0.62$; model B has 0.55.
quiz.question: Which will forecast next year's returns better?

options.text: We cannot tell from these numbers: test both on data they were not fitted to
Model A, because its adjusted $R^2$ is higher
options.why: You read adjusted $R^2$ as forecast skill. It penalises predictors, but it is still measured on the fitting data.

options.text: Model B, because a lower $R^2$ means less overfitting
options.why: A lower in-sample fit is no guarantee of a better forecast either.

options.text: Both equally, because both are significant
options.why: Significance in sample says nothing about which forecasts better.

feedback.correct: Forecasting skill is measured out of sample.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which data the adjusted $R^2$ was measured on.

explain.text: Adjusted $R^2$ charges for predictors, but it is still computed on the data used to fit. A model tuned to the past can lose out of sample. Only a hold-out test settles it.
